title: Laxatives, prokinetics and antidiarrhoeals: what changes stool movement
ariaLabel: Schematic of gut transit: propulsive movement of the gut wall, water kept in the lumen, and fluid secreted by the gut lining all add to stool frequency. Stimulant laxatives and prokinetics increase propulsion, osmotic laxatives hold water in the gut, opioid antidiarrhoeals such as loperamide reduce propulsion, and antisecretory drugs lower fluid secretion.
caption: Schematic, not to scale. Flow and levels are qualitative and illustrative; no dose, concentration or lipid value is shown or implied.

edges.label: propulsion
edges.info: Prokinetics (metoclopramide, domperidone) and stimulant laxatives (senna, bisacodyl) raise propulsion; loperamide acts on opioid receptors of the gut to lower it.
Adds to the effect shown at the right.

edges.label: luminal water
edges.info: Osmotic laxatives (lactulose, macrogol, magnesium salts) keep water in the lumen and soften stool. Bulk-forming agents also hold water.
Adds to the effect shown at the right.

edges.label: secretion
edges.info: Racecadotril lowers secretion by blocking enkephalinase; stimulant laxatives raise it. Cholera toxin drives it.
Adds to the effect shown at the right.

sources: Where each class acts. Stimulant laxatives raise propulsion, osmotic laxatives hold water in the gut, loperamide lowers propulsion, and antisecretory drugs lower fluid secretion. This is standard teaching in the pharmacology texts the PrepNucleus lessons cite (Katzung; KD Tripathi) and were not checked against a linked source here, so they are flagged for review.
simplified: Oral rehydration, causes of diarrhoea and constipation, antibiotics and infection, bulk-forming and lubricant laxatives, lubiprostone and linaclotide, 5-HT3 and 5-HT4 drugs, contraindications (toxic megacolon, infective diarrhoea), adverse effects and electrolyte loss are left out. Stool frequency is drawn as a teaching score. Levels and the size of each effect are illustrative. The drug choices are teaching toggles of a class: no named drug, dose or schedule is shown or implied, and the figure does not say who should or should not take any of them.
